title: Adab of travel
hookLine: a verse for setting off, company on the road, and praise on the way home

lines: A DESTINATION NOT ON THE MAP.
cards: The seatbelt clicks. The engine turns over. And before the car pulls out, the driver says a line under her breath, in Arabic.
It isn't a line about cars. It comes from the Qur'an, from a passage about riding animals and ships, written long before any engine. Partway through, it admits something.
It ends by mentioning a destination that isn't on any map in the car. Today: the manners of leaving home, and of coming back.

teach.h: WE WERE NOT CAPABLE OF IT.
teach.b: Ibn 'Umar describes it in Sahih Muslim. When the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, mounted his camel to set out on a journey, he said Allahu akbar three times, then recited two verses of al-Zukhruf.

teach.h: UNTO OUR LORD WE ARE RETURNING.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us, and we were not capable (of subduing them); And lo! unto our Lord we surely are returning." The admission first: we were not capable.
The animal, the ship, today the car or the plane: none of it is ours by our own strength. Then the turn: unto our Lord we are returning.
Every trip has a return built in, and the verse points past it to the last return of all. In the same report, he asked for goodness on the journey and for the distance to be made easy.
Coming home, he said it again and added: returning, repenting, worshipping, praising our Lord. Two more pieces.
Company: a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says, in paraphrase, that if people knew what he knew about traveling alone, no rider would travel alone at night.
And home: another hadith in Bukhari calls travel a piece of torment, because it keeps a person from food, drink and sleep, so when your business is done, hurry back to your family. Leave remembering.
Travel with others where you can. Come home quickly, praising.

how: Muslims setting out on a journey say Allahu akbar and recite the verses of al-Zukhruf, "Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us," in Arabic, and on returning add words of praise.

o: a pilgrimage made only to Mecca and Medina
remembering Allah as you set out and come home
packing light and never traveling far from home

games.q: the adab of travel — tap the pairs.
p: no rider would, if they knew
so hurry home when it's done

s: the travel du'a was written about roads and cars
it comes from al-Zukhruf, about the animals and ships Allah subdued for people.
the Prophet said words of praise on the way home too
returning, repenting, worshipping, praising our Lord.
the hadith praises riding alone at night
it says if people knew what he knew, no rider would travel alone at night.

games.q: your trip's business is done a day early. by the hadith, what does the adab of travel suggest?
o: stay on alone and see the sights.
games.why: travel is a piece of torment, the hadith says, keeping a person from food, drink and sleep: when your business is done, hurry home.

practice: Picture the next trip you'll take, even across town, and see yourself sitting down in the seat.

If you pray, you can say the words now, in Arabic if you know them, or in English: Glorified be He Who hath subdued these unto us; if you don't, just notice how much of the trip you didn't build, the road, the engine, the hands that made them.
Then see yourself walking back through your own door, and stay with that return.

wordCard.voice: Adab of travel. The manners of the road: remember Allah setting out, keep company where you can, and come home quickly, praising. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: journey, travel; a traveler is a musafir.

carryVoice: Your line: travel remembering. Every trip has a return built in. Until tomorrow.
